title: The lion and the breath
hookLine: a fish overhears Shiva teaching yoga, and the manual that follows says tame the breath like a lion
carry: steady breath, steady mind, learned from a guru

lines: A LION, AN ELEPHANT, A TIGER.
cards: There's a legend in the Nath yogis' tradition about how hatha yoga reached people. Shiva was teaching yoga to Parvati by the sea, and a great fish lay listening in the water; in many tellings, a child was inside it.
Every word went in, and out came a master: Matsyendra, lord of the fish.
The Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a manual for yogis, opens with a bow to Adinatha, the first lord, Shiva, and names Matsyendra among the masters who handed the practice down.
Then, in chapter two, where it starts teaching breath, it brings in a lion, an elephant and a tiger.

teach.b: Chapter two, verse fifteen, in paraphrase: as a lion, an elephant or a tiger is brought under control slowly, little by little, so the breath is brought under control. Otherwise, it harms the one who practices.
The next verse adds that breath practice done properly helps, and done wrongly brings illness. The warning is about pace.
A few verses earlier, the chapter gives the reason breath matters at all: when the breath moves unsteadily, the mind is unsteady; when the breath is still, the mind is still.
That's the hatha tradition's big teaching: breath and mind move together, so steadying one steadies the other. And it's why the manual keeps naming its teachers.

teach.h: PARAMPARA: FROM SHIVA, GURU TO STUDENT.
teach.b: Hatha yoga comes down as a parampara, a line of gurus reaching back, in the tradition's own telling, to Shiva.

teach.h: LONG HOLDS, LEARNED WITH A GURU.
teach.b: A lion isn't tamed from a book, and the stronger practices, long holds especially, are traditionally learned one to one, with a guru watching.
Teachers call the pace krama, going in order, though the verse doesn't use the word.
This week has followed that line: the breath the others rise with, the limbs before the breath, breath offered into breath, and now the pace.
It began with the Ashtavakra Gita, where the sage tells Janaka that practicing meditation is itself his bondage; the hatha manual is practice from start to finish.

how: In hatha yoga lineages, practice is received from a guru, and some sessions open with a bow to Adinatha, Shiva; breath practices are learned in order, gentle ones first, with longer holds left until later and sometimes taught one to one by a teacher who watches the student.

o: long breath holds practiced from the very first day
a set of poses named for the lion and the tiger
breath practice built slowly, gentle steps before long holds

games.q: the lion and the breath — tap the pairs.
p: Shiva, the first teacher of hatha yoga
the fish who overheard Shiva, in the Nath legend

s: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika says breath practice is risk-free
it warns that breath forced too fast can harm, the way an untamed animal can.
the same chapter links a still breath with a still mind
it says when the breath moves unsteadily the mind is unsteady, and when the breath is still the mind is still.
the Hatha Yoga Pradipika treats breath practice as something to pick up alone from a book
it opens by bowing to Adinatha, Shiva, and names a line of masters; the practice comes down from guru to student.

games.q: you're new to breath practice and you've read about long breath holds. where do you start?
o: with the longest hold you can manage.
with gentle, slow breathing, holds left for later.
with whatever looks hardest, to save time.
games.why: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika compares the breath to a lion tamed little by little, warns that rushing it harms, and the stronger practices come from a teacher.

practice: If you pray, begin as the manual does, with a bow to the first teacher, or to your own. Start with a few breaths as they come, then a gentle count: in for four, out for four.
When that's easy, stretch only the out-breath to five or six, and if the chest, throat or jaw strains, return to the even count; that return is part of the sequence, not a failure of it.
Near the end, drop the counting and let the breath settle by itself.

wordCard.voice: Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the pace of that order: little by little, the way a lion is tamed, under a guru's eye.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: krama, a step, a going in order; the idea behind any sequence.

carryVoice: Your line: steady breath, steady mind, learned from a guru. Little by little, the way a lion is tamed. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Matsyendra overhearing Shiva teach Parvati, as a fish
